messages.subject: Estimating the proportion of observations in an unknown population that fall outside an interval constructed on the basis of a sample from it
messages.subject_clean: Estimating the proportion of observations in an unknown population that fall outside an interval constructed on the basis of a sample from it
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I’m working on a problem and I was hoping any of you might have any 
pointers for me (including, if applicable, “this can’t be done”). Sorry 
for the length.

In second language acquisition, researchers sometimes wish to quantify 
how many second-language (L2) speakers in their sample are “nativelike”. 
This is done by comparing their performance on a battery of tasks to 
that of a sample of L1 speakers. Using the native speaker data, 
“nativelike intervals” are constructed. Two common ways to do this are 
(a) to define these intervals as the native sample’s ranges and (b) to 
define them as the native sample means +/- 2 standard deviations. 
Typically, L2 speakers are considered potentially nativelike if their 
performance falls within the nativelikeness interval for all tasks.

In my view, a major problem with this strategy is that it is possible 
that some native speakers - even ones drawn from the sample population 
as the native controls - will fail to perform within the thusly defined 
nativelikeness interval for all tasks. This possibility exists if the 
nativelikeness interval underestimates the performance range within the 
population from which the native controls were sampled. And if, say, 10% 
of L1 speakers would fail to perform within all nativelikeness 
intervals, then, in principle, it’s possible that 10% of the L2 speakers 
identified as non-nativelike ought to be considered nativelike, too.

Let’s call the proportion of L1 speakers who don’t perform within all 
nativelikeness intervals the battery’s “miss rate”. For the sake of 
simplicity, let’s further assume that the task scores are all 
intercorrelated at “r” within the L1 population and are all normally 
distributed. Also, let’s assume that SLA researchers have their reasons 
for constructing such intervals rather than using more refined 
classification algorithms.* On the basis of these simplifying 
assumptions, miss rates for different scenarios (size of the native 
control sample, number of tasks in battery, different intercorrelations) 
can be computed using simulations: draw a sample of size n from the 
multivariate normal distribution, compute intervals, draw a large sample 
from the same distribution, and see how many observations don’t fall in 
all intervals.

The above is, I hope, sufficient to convince people that these miss 
rates exist and that they can be pretty large, especially if the control 
samples are small and the number of tasks is largish. What would be 
great, however, is *if **you**could **use the sample of native controls 
you recruited to estimate the miss rate of the set of intervals that you 
constructed on the basis of them*.

Does anyone have any ideas about how to go about this? To make this 
concrete, let’s say your native sample of size 10, assumed to be drawn 
randomly from some population of L1 speakers (a multivariate normal 
distribution), has the following task scores:

native_sample <- structure(c(0.435549035598253, -0.733233794669011, 
1.11031819215666, -1.42156636159226, -0.470466348416922, 
-0.344544376519479, -3.16140380323258, 1.25911320034122, 
-0.505015560013396, -0.27245327626564, 0.69950457554912, 
-0.549955837569371, 0.804997707814359, -0.308465377431691, 
-0.0686566378218331, 0.55621330641487, -2.15129256390727, 
1.51382617869646, -0.800769937952146, 0.0695413334342196, 
0.906269766423279, 0.468478559989297, 1.4336687374579, 
-1.55045691958889, -0.962196997062294, -0.491428475600102, 
-1.05473041129592, 1.96984949987731, -0.364288431419078, 
-0.501212009426657), .Dim = c(10L, 3L), .Dimnames = list(NULL, NULL))

The range-based intervals are:

[, 1]: [-3.16; 1.26]
[, 2]: [-2.15; 1.51]
[, 3]: [-1.55; 1.97]


The SD-based intervals are:

[, 1]: [-2.95; 2.13]
[, 2]: [-2.07; 2.02]
[, 3]: [-2.33; 2.30]

Is it possible to estimate the proportion of observations in the 
population from which native_sample was sampled that doesn’t fall in all 
three intervals? (I don't think it's possible for a single task, but 
perhaps it's paradoxically possible if there are several tasks.)

Thanks for your time,

Jan


(*) I could imagine using, say, random forests to assess how well the L1 
speakers can be separated from the L2 speakers on the basis of the task 
scores. This would yield an estimate of the classification’s miss rate 
(L1 speakers mistaken for L2 speakers) and of the prevalence of 
nativelikeness (L2 speakers mistaken for L1 speakers). But I think (not 
sure) that some SLA researchers might object that operationalisations of 
nativelikeness shouldn’t depend on the L2 speakers’ data.

messages.body_plain:
Hello List,

 

I am currently working on a production data set that has undergone forced
alignment.

I can identify cases where alignment might be bad, and I want to look at
them in Praat.

 

I have the filenames in R and I want to open the wav and textgrid file in
Praat.

I have tried PraatR, but it does not support a simple "Read from file"
command.

Any other ideas?

 

Thanks in advance,

Holger

messages.subject: Re: opening an sound and TextGrid in Praat from R
messages.subject_clean: opening an sound and TextGrid in Praat from R
messages.body_plain:
Hi Holger, try this:

audio <- "path/to/audio.wav"
textgrid <- "path/to/textgrid.TextGrid"
command <- paste(c("praat", "--open", audio, textgrid), collapse=" ")
system(command)

It will not pop open the editor window, but it will at least launch praat
and load the files into the object window for you.  More info here:
http://www.fon.hum.uva.nl/praat/manual/Scripting_6_9__Calling_from_the_command_line.html

-- dan

Daniel McCloy
http://dan.mccloy.info/
Postdoctoral Research Associate
Institute for Learning and Brain Sciences
University of Washington

Hi Holger,

Unfortunately I can't reproduce the error you're seeing.  Searching for "r
system error 127" yields this StackOverflow answer:
https://stackoverflow.com/a/33647207/1664024
suggesting that you should use R's "shell" command in lieu of R's "system"
command.  I cannot confirm that this will work for you, as I'm not running
Windows.  I'm cc-ing the mailing list so that windows users can take over
any further troubleshooting help.

-- dan
